==Problem==
Let <imath>x_0,x_1,x_2,\dotsc</imath> be a sequence of numbers, where each <imath>x_k</imath> is either <imath>0</imath> or <imath>1</imath>. For each positive integer <imath>n</imath>, define 
<cmath>S_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} x_k 2^k</cmath>
Suppose <imath>7S_n \equiv 1 \pmod{2^n}</imath> for all <imath>n \geq 1</imath>. What is the value of the sum  
<cmath>x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022}?</cmath>
<imath>\textbf{(A) } 6 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 7 \qquad \textbf{(C) }12\qquad \textbf{(D) } 14\qquad \textbf{(E) }15</imath>

==Solution 1==

In binary numbers, we have <cmath>S_n = (x_{n-1} x_{n-2} x_{n-3} x_{n-4} \ldots x_{2} x_{1} x_{0})_2.</cmath>
It follows that <cmath>8S_n = (x_{n-1} x_{n-2} x_{n-3} x_{n-4} \ldots x_{2} x_{1} x_{0}000)_2.</cmath>
We obtain <imath>7S_n</imath> by subtracting the equations:
<cmath>\begin{array}{clccrccccccr}
  & (x_{n-1} & x_{n-2} & x_{n-3} & x_{n-4} & \ldots & x_2 & x_1 & x_0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \ )_2 \\
-\quad & & & & (x_{n-1} & \ldots & x_5 & x_4 & x_3 & x_2 & x_1 & x_0)_2 \\
\hline
  & & & & & & & & & & &  \\ [-2.5ex]
  & ( \ \ ?& ? & ? & 0 \ \ \ & \ldots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \ )_2 \\
\end{array}</cmath>
We work from right to left:
<cmath>\begin{alignat*}{6}
x_0=x_1=x_2=1 
\quad &\implies \quad &x_3 &= 0& \\ 
\quad &\implies \quad &x_4 &= 1& \\ 
\quad &\implies \quad &x_5 &= 1& \\
\quad &\implies \quad &x_6 &= 0& \\ 
\quad &\implies \quad &x_7 &= 1& \\ 
\quad &\implies \quad &x_8 &= 1& \\
\quad &\quad \vdots & & &
\end{alignat*}</cmath>
For all <imath>n\geq3,</imath> we conclude that

* <imath>x_n=0</imath> if and only if <imath>n\equiv 0\pmod{3}.</imath>

* <imath>x_n=1</imath> if and only if <imath>n\not\equiv 0\pmod{3}.</imath>

Finally, we get <imath>(x_{2019},x_{2020},x_{2021},x_{2022})=(0,1,1,0),</imath> from which <cmath>x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022} = \boxed{\textbf{(A) } 6}.</cmath>
~Steven Chen (Professor Chen Education Palace, www.professorchenedu.com)

~MRENTHUSIASM

==Solution 2==
First, notice that <cmath>x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022} = \frac{S_{2023} - S_{2019}}{2^{2019}}.</cmath>
Then since <imath>S_n</imath> is the modular inverse of <imath>7</imath> in <imath>\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}</imath>, we can perform the Euclidean Algorithm to find it for <imath>n = 2019,2023</imath>.

Starting with <imath>2019</imath>, 
<cmath>\begin{align*}
7S_{2019} &\equiv 1 \pmod{2^{2019}} \\
7S_{2019} &= 2^{2019}k + 1.
\end{align*}</cmath>
Now, take both sides <imath>\operatorname{mod} \ 7</imath>:
<cmath>0 \equiv 2^{2019}k + 1 \pmod{7}.</cmath>
Using Fermat's Little Theorem, <cmath>2^{2019} = (2^{336})^6 \cdot 2^3 \equiv 2^3 \equiv 1 \pmod{7}.</cmath>
Thus,  <cmath>0 \equiv k + 1 \pmod{7} \implies k \equiv 6 \pmod{7} \implies k = 7j + 6.</cmath>
Therefore, <cmath>7S_{2019} = 2^{2019} (7j + 6) + 1 \implies S_{2019} = \frac{2^{2019} (7j + 6) + 1}{7}.</cmath>

We may repeat this same calculation with <imath>S_{2023}</imath> to yield <cmath>S_{2023} = \frac{2^{2023} (7h + 3) + 1}{7}.</cmath>
Now, we notice that <imath>S_n</imath> is basically an integer expressed in binary form with <imath>n</imath> bits.
This gives rise to a simple inequality, <cmath>0 \leqslant S_n \leqslant 2^n.</cmath>
Since the maximum possible number that can be generated with <imath>n</imath> bits is <cmath>\underbrace{{11111\dotsc1}_2}_{n} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} 2^k = 2^n - 1 \leqslant 2^n.</cmath>
Looking at our calculations for <imath>S_{2019}</imath> and <imath>S_{2023}</imath>, we see that the only valid integers that satisfy that constraint are <imath>j = h = 0</imath>.
<cmath>\frac{S_{2023} - S_{2019}}{2^{2019}} = \frac{\tfrac{2^{2023} \cdot 3 + 1}{7} - \tfrac{2^{2019} \cdot 6 + 1}{7}}{2^{2019}} = \frac{2^4 \cdot 3 - 6}{7} = \boxed{\textbf{(A) } 6}.</cmath>
~zoomanTV

==Solution 3 ==

As in Solution 2, we note that 
<cmath>x_{2019}+2x_{2020}+4x_{2021}+8x_{2022}=\frac{S_{2023}-S_{2019}}{2^{2019}}.</cmath>
We also know that <imath>7S_{2023} \equiv 1 \pmod{2^{2023}}</imath> and <imath>7S_{2019} \equiv 1 \pmod{2^{2019}}</imath>, this implies:
<cmath> \textbf{(1) } 7S_{2023}=2^{2023}\cdot{x} + 1, </cmath>
<cmath> \textbf{(2) } 7S_{2019}=2^{2019}\cdot{y} + 1. </cmath>
Dividing by <imath>7</imath>, we can isolate the previous sums:
<cmath> \textbf{(3) } S_{2023}=\frac{2^{2023}\cdot{x} + 1}{7}, </cmath>
<cmath> \textbf{(4) } S_{2019}=\frac{2^{2019}\cdot{y} + 1}{7}. </cmath>
The maximum value of <imath>S_n</imath> occurs when every <imath>x_i</imath> is equal to <imath>1</imath>. Even when this happens, the value of <imath>S_n</imath> is less than <imath>2^n</imath>. Therefore, we can construct the following inequalities:
<cmath> \textbf{(3) } S_{2023}=\frac{2^{2023}\cdot{x} + 1}{7} < 2^{2023}, </cmath>
<cmath> \textbf{(4) } S_{2019}=\frac{2^{2019}\cdot{y} + 1}{7} < 2^{2019}. </cmath>
From these two equations, we can deduce that both <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> are less than <imath>7</imath>. 

Reducing <imath>\textbf{1}</imath> and <imath>\textbf{2}</imath> <imath>\pmod{7},</imath> we see that 
<cmath>2^{2023}\cdot{x}\equiv 6\pmod{7},</cmath>
and 
<cmath>2^{2019}\cdot{y}\equiv 6\pmod{7}.</cmath>

The powers of <imath>2</imath> repeat every <imath>3, \pmod{7}.</imath> 

Therefore, <imath>2^{2023}\equiv 2 \pmod 7</imath> and <imath>2^{2019} \equiv 1 \pmod {7}.</imath> Substituing this back into the above equations, 
<cmath>2x\equiv{6}\pmod{7}</cmath>
and
<cmath>y\equiv{6}\pmod{7}.</cmath>

Since <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> are integers less than <imath>7</imath>, the only values of <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> are <imath>3</imath> and <imath>6</imath> respectively. 

The requested sum is 
<cmath>\begin{align*}
\frac{S_{2023}-S_{2019}}{2^{2019}} &= \frac{\frac{2^{2023}\cdot{x} + 1}{7} - \frac{2^{2019}\cdot{y} + 1}{7}}{2^{2019}} \\
&= \frac{1}{2^{2019}}\left(\frac{2^{2023}\cdot{3} + 1}{7} -\left(\frac{2^{2019}\cdot{6} + 1}{7}  \right)\right) \\
&= \frac{3\cdot{2^4}-6}{7} \\
&= \boxed{\textbf{(A) } 6}.
\end{align*}</cmath>
-Benedict T (countmath1)

==Solution 4 ==

Note that, as in Solution 2, we have <cmath>x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022} = \frac{S_{2023} - S_{2019}}{2^{2019}}.</cmath> This is because <cmath>S_{2023} = x_{0}2^{0} + x_{1}2^{1} + \cdots + x_{2019}2^{2019} + \cdots + x_{2022}2^{2022}</cmath> and <cmath>S_{2019} = x_{0}2^{0} + x_{1}2^{1} + \cdots + x_{2018}2^{2018}.</cmath> Note that <cmath>S_{2023} - S_{2019} = x_{2019}2^{2019} + \cdots + x_{2022}2^{2022} = 2^{2019}(x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022}).</cmath> Therefore, <cmath>x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022} = \frac{S_{2023} - S_{2019}}{2^{2019}}.</cmath> Multiplying both sides by 7 gives us <cmath>7(x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022}) = \frac{7S_{2023} - 7S_{2019}}{2^{2019}}.</cmath> We can write <cmath>7S_{2023} = 1\pmod{2^{2023}} = 1 + 2^{2023}a = 1 + 2^{2019}*16a</cmath> and <cmath>7S_{2019} = 1\pmod{2^{2019}} = 1 + 2^{2019}b</cmath> for some a and b. Substituting, we get <cmath>7(x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022}) = \frac{(1 + 2^{2019} * 16a) - (1 + 2^{2019}b)}{2^{2019}} = 16a - b.</cmath> Therefore, our answer can be written as <cmath>\frac{16a - b}{7}.</cmath> Another thing to notice is that a and b are integers between 0 and 6. This is because <cmath>7(1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + \cdots + 2^{2022}) \geqslant 7S_{2023} = 1 + 2^{2023}a</cmath> which is <cmath>7(2^{2023}) - 7 \geqslant 1 + 2^{2023}a</cmath> <cmath>(7-a) \geqslant \frac{8}{2^{2023}}</cmath> which only holds when a is less than 7 because the right is very small positive number, so the left must be positive, too. Clearly, a is also non-negative, because otherwise, <cmath>7S_{2023} = 1 + 2^{2023}a < 0</cmath> which would mean <cmath>S_{2023} < 0</cmath> which cannot happen, so a is greater than 0.  A similar explanation for b shows that b is an integer between 0 and 6 inclusive. 

Going back to the solution, if our answer to the problem is n, then <cmath>16a - b = 7n</cmath> and <cmath>16a = 7n + b,</cmath> so we can try the five option choices and see which one, when multiplied by 7 and added to some whole number between 0 and 6 results in a multiple of 16. Trying all the option choices, we see that you need to add 7n to something more than 6 to equal a multiple of 16 other than for option A. Therefore, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) } 6}.</imath>

-Rutvik Arora (youtube channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCkgAgmNAQV8WGTOazGYEGwg)

==Solution 5 ==

Given that <imath>7S_n \equiv 1 \pmod{2^n}</imath>, we have
<cmath>\begin{align*}
7S_n &= a_n2^n + 1\\
7S_{n-1} &= a_{n-1}2^{n-1} + 1.
\end{align*}</cmath>
where <imath>a_n</imath> is integer.

Notice that <cmath>S_n = S_{n-1} + 2^{n-1}x_{n-1}.</cmath>
Thus,
<cmath>\begin{align*}
7(S_n - S_{n-1}) &= 2^{n-1}(2a_n - a_{n-1})\\
7 \cdot 2^{n - 1}x_{n - 1} &= 2^{n - 1}(2a_n - a_{n - 1})\\
7x_{n-1} &= 2a_n - a_{n-1}.
\end{align*}</cmath>
Obviously, <imath>x_0 = 1</imath>, <imath>S_1 = 1</imath>, <imath>7S_1 = 3 \times 2^1 + 1</imath>, so <imath>a_1 = 3</imath>. 
For each <imath>i</imath>, <imath>x_i</imath> must be 0 or 1, and <imath>a_i</imath> is an integer, so we can repeat the recursion to yield
<cmath>\begin{align*}
x_1 = \frac{2a_2 - a_1}{7} = \frac{2a_2 - 3}{7}\text{ can only be 1, where }a_2 = 5\\
x_2 = \frac{2a_3 - a_2}{7} = \frac{2a_3 - 5}{7}\text{ can only be 1, where }a_3 = 6\\
x_3 = \frac{2a_4 - a_3}{7} = \frac{2a_4 - 6}{7}\text{ can only be 0, where }a_4 = 3\\
x_4 = \frac{2a_5 - a_4}{7} = \frac{2a_5 - 3}{7}\text{ can only be 1, where }a_5 = 5\\
x_5 = \frac{2a_6 - a_5}{7} = \frac{2a_6 - 5}{7}\text{ can only be 1, where }a_6 = 6\\
x_6 = \frac{2a_7 - a_6}{7} = \frac{2a_7 - 6}{7}\text{ can only be 0, where }a_7 = 3
\end{align*}</cmath>
So for any non-negative integer <imath>k</imath>,  we can find that <imath>x_{3k + 1} = 1</imath>, <imath>x_{3k + 2} = 1</imath>, <imath>x_{3k + 3} = 0</imath>, <cmath>x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022} = 0 + 2 \times 1 + 4 \times 1 + 8 \times  0 = \boxed{\textbf{(A) } 6}.</cmath>

~[https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/User:Reda_mandymath reda_mandymath]

==Solution 6==

Using the given conditions, it is evident that <imath>x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022}=\frac{S_{2023}-S_{2019}}{2^{2019}}=a</imath> (for simplicity). Moreover, because <imath>7S_n \equiv 1 \pmod{2^n}</imath> is true, an impulse to multiply the numerator and denominator by 7 is created. Let <imath>7S_{2023}=2^{2023}k+1</imath> and <imath>7S_{2019}=2^{2019}k'+1</imath>.
\begin{align*}
a=\frac{7S_{2023}-7S_{2019}}{7\cdot2^{2019}}&=\frac{2^{2023}k+1-2^{2019}k'-1}{7\cdot2^{2019}} \\
&=\frac{2^4k-k'}{7} \\
&=\frac{16k-k'}{7} \\
\end{align*}
Furthermore, because <imath>0\le x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022}\le15</imath>, <imath>0\le\frac{16k-k'}{7}\le15</imath>. The order pairs <imath>(k,k',a)</imath> could be found through trial and error that satisfies conditions <imath>7S_{2023}=2^{2023}k+1</imath> and <imath>7S_{2019}=2^{2019}k'+1</imath>. It is evident that <imath>k\ne0,1,2</imath> using Euler's Theorem.

<imath>(3,6,6)</imath> is valid because <imath>7|2^{2023}\cdot3+1</imath> and <imath>7|2^{2019}\cdot6</imath>.
Thereby, <imath>x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022}=\boxed{\textbf{(A) } 6}</imath>.

~MaPhyCom

==Solution 7 (Very Fast but Still Rigorous)==

<imath>7=2^3-1 | 2^{2022}-1</imath> since <imath>3|2022</imath>, so <imath>2^{2022} \equiv 1 \pmod 7</imath>, with 
<cmath>2^{2022}-1 = 7 (2^{2019} + 2^ {2016} + \dots +1).</cmath>
<imath>6 \cdot 2^{2022} +1</imath> thus is a multiple of <imath>7</imath>, so it is thus <imath>7 \cdot S_n</imath>. We have
<cmath>6 \cdot 2^{2022} +1 = (2^2+2^1) (7 (2^{2019} + 2^ {2016} + \dots +1) +1) +1 = 7 ((2^2+2^1)(2^{2019} + 2^ {2016} + \dots +1) +1) = 7 (2^{2021}+ 2^{2020} + 2^{2018}+2^{2017}+\dots),</cmath>
so <imath>x_{2022}=0,x_{2021}=1, x_{2020}=1, x_{2019}=0 \implies x_{2019} + 2x_{2020} + 4x_{2021} + 8x_{2022}=\boxed{\textbf{(A) } 6}</imath>.

~[[Ddk001]]

==Solution 8 (Binary but very fast in practice)==

Notice that <imath>S_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} x_k 2^k</imath> represents the binary representation of the integer which consists of the digits <imath>x_{n-1} x_{n-2} \ldots x_{0}</imath>.
The given condition states that <cmath>7S_{n} \equiv 1 \pmod {2^{n}}</cmath>
Thus, <cmath>S_{n} \equiv 7^{-1} \pmod {2^{n}}</cmath><cmath>\equiv -\frac{1}{1-2^{3}} \pmod {2^{n}}</cmath>
Using the geometric series expansion for 2-adics: <cmath>\frac{1}{1-2^{3}}=1+2^{3}+2^{6}+2^{9}+\ldots</cmath>
Remember that <imath>-n=\sim n+1</imath>, or, in words, the negative of a number is formed by taking its bitwise complement and adding one. (Explanation below) <imath>\newline</imath>
And so,  <cmath>-\frac{1}{1-2^{3}}=(1+2^{1}+2^{2}+2^{4}+2^{5}+\ldots)</cmath>
This directly gives us <cmath>x_{0}=1,x_{1}=1,x_{2}=1</cmath><cmath>x_{3}=0</cmath> and generally if <imath>k \equiv 0 \pmod 3</imath>,<imath>x_{1}=0</imath> and if <imath>k \not\equiv 0 \pmod 3</imath>, <imath>x_{k}=1.</imath><imath>\newline</imath> 
Substituting this into our target sum, <cmath>x_{2019}+2x_{2020}+4x_{2021}+8x_{2022}=0+2(1)+4(1)+8(0)=\boxed{\textbf{(A) } 6}.</cmath>

==Note==<imath>\newline</imath>The bitwise complement of a binary number is the result of "flipping" every bit, changing <imath>1</imath>'s to <imath>0</imath>'s and <imath>0</imath>'s to <imath>1</imath>'s. Thus, adding the complement of a number to itself adds <imath>0</imath>'s to the <imath>1</imath>'s and <imath>1</imath>'s to the <imath>0</imath>'s, which gives a string of all ones, represented by <imath>-1</imath> in the 2-adic world. This can be expressed as <imath>n+\sim n=-1</imath>, and rearranging gives us <imath>-n=\sim n+1</imath> <imath>\newline</imath> Ex:
<cmath>13=\ldots001101_{2}</cmath><cmath>13+\sim 13=\ldots001101_{2}+\ldots110010_{2}=\ldots111111_{2}</cmath><imath>\newline</imath>
~larryliao
